en: Striking; catching attention
hook: ARRESTING: it ARRESTS your attention — you can't move on.
story: The photograph of a girl reading under a streetlight in the rain was so arresting that people stopped in the gallery for minutes, unable to look away. Arresting means strikingly attention-grabbing. It's a compliment, not a police matter.

en: To scold or criticize severely
hook: CHASTISE: CHASE them with words until they're CHASTE (corrected).
story: The coach chastised the striker for missing training three times in a week: 'Talent without discipline is useless!' To chastise is to scold sharply. Synonyms: castigate, upbraid, rebuke.

en: Difficult to handle because of size, weight, or complexity
hook: CUMBERSOME: ENCUMBERS you, weighing you down.
story: Arif's old laptop was cumbersome: four kilograms, a huge charger, and a battery that died in an hour. Carrying it to class every day hurt his back. Cumbersome means awkward to handle. The bank's process was cumbersome too: five forms to change one address.

en: Careful management of resources; thrift and efficiency in use
hook: GRE trick: ECONOMY of words means using no more words than needed.
story: The poet wrote with great economy: every word did work, and not one was wasted. Grandma's household economy was impressive too; she fed eight people on a tiny budget. On the GRE, economy means careful, efficient use, especially of words or resources.

en: Basic; relating to the simplest beginning stages
hook: ELEMENTARY: the basic ELEMENTS.
story: 'Elementary, my dear Watson,' Sherlock Holmes would say, explaining a clue that seemed simple once revealed. Elementary means basic and fundamental. Elementary school teaches the foundations: reading, writing, and arithmetic.

en: To decorate; to add details, often untrue, to make a story more interesting
hook: EMBELLISH: add BELLS to it, decorate.
story: Each time Uncle Jamal told his fishing story, he embellished it: the fish grew from two kilos to five, then ten, then a giant that pulled the boat. To embellish is to decorate or exaggerate. Embroidered saris are embellished with beads and gold thread.

en: Feeling intense happiness and excitement
hook: EUPHORIC: feeling EU-phoria, extreme 'yay!'
story: When Bangladesh won the match in the final over, the whole country was euphoric: people danced in the streets, hugged strangers, and waved flags until dawn. Euphoric means intensely happy. Synonyms: elated, ecstatic, jubilant.

en: To officially clear someone from blame
hook: EX-ONERATE: remove the ONUS (burden) of guilt.
story: After spending eight years in prison, the man was finally exonerated when DNA evidence proved someone else committed the crime. To exonerate is to clear from blame. Synonyms: exculpate, absolve, vindicate.

en: To estimate unknown values by extending known trends
hook: EXTRA-POLATE: extend the line EXTRA far beyond the data.
story: Nadia's scores rose ten points every month. Extrapolating from that trend, she predicted she'd reach 325 by test day. To extrapolate is to infer future or unknown values from known data. But beware: trends don't always continue.

en: To lose strength or momentum; to hesitate
hook: FALTER: like a FAULT in your step.
story: Halfway through her speech, Sara's voice faltered when she saw her late father's photo on the wall. She paused, took a breath, and continued. To falter is to hesitate or lose strength. A faltering economy is slowing down.

en: Having or showing intense passion
hook: FERVENT: burning with FERVOR.
story: Tanvir is a fervent supporter of the national team; he watches every match, even at three in the morning, and paints his face for the big games. Fervent means intensely passionate. A fervent prayer comes from the heart.

en: To stir up trouble or rebellion
hook: FOMENT: FERMENT trouble, let it bubble.
story: Agitators spread false rumors on social media to foment violence between two communities. To foment is to instigate trouble. Synonyms: incite, provoke, instigate. Don't confuse it with ferment, though they are related.

en: An embarrassing social mistake
hook: GAFFE: a GAFFE makes everyone LAUGH at you.
story: At the wedding, Rafi congratulated the bride's father on his 'second marriage.' It was actually his first. The whole table went silent at the gaffe. A gaffe is an embarrassing blunder, especially in a social situation.

en: Not conforming to accepted or orthodox beliefs
hook: HETERO-DOX: DIFFERENT belief (orthodox = correct belief).
story: The economist held heterodox views; he argued that the country should print more money, against all mainstream advice. Some called him a genius, others a fool. Heterodox means unorthodox, going against accepted beliefs.

en: Overly theatrical or dramatic in behavior
hook: HISTRIONIC: like a HISTORIC actor overacting.
story: When asked to wash the dishes, Arif's little sister fell to the floor, clutched her heart, and wailed, 'Why is life so cruel?' Her histrionic display made everyone laugh. Histrionic means excessively dramatic, like a bad actor.

en: Implied though not directly expressed; absolute and unquestioning
hook: IMPLICIT: IMPLIED. Opposite: EXPLICIT.
story: Her mother never said, 'Don't come home late.' But the message was implicit in her worried face at the door. Implicit means implied rather than stated. Implicit trust means total, unquestioning trust. Its opposite is explicit.

en: Free from injury or violation; untouched
hook: IN-VIOLATE: NOT VIOLATED.
story: For Nadia, her Friday family dinner was inviolate; no exam, no friend, no party could make her skip it. Inviolate means never broken or violated. Some forests remain inviolate, untouched by human hands.

en: Something that puts one at a disadvantage; legal responsibility
hook: LIABILITY: something you're LIABLE for, a burden.
story: The star player's temper became a liability; he got red cards in three straight matches, hurting his team. A liability is a disadvantage or burden. In law, it means legal responsibility. Its opposite is an asset.

en: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion
hook: OBSTINATE: an OBSTACLE that won't move.
story: The obstinate goat refused to cross the bridge. Pulling, pushing, offering grass: nothing worked. Grandpa was just as obstinate, refusing to see a doctor for weeks. Obstinate means stubbornly unyielding. Synonyms: intransigent, pertinacious, mulish.

en: Done with or employing great care and thoroughness
hook: PAINS-TAKING: TAKING great PAINS.
story: The restorer spent three years on painstaking work, cleaning the ancient painting one tiny square at a time with a cotton swab. Painstaking means extremely careful and thorough. Synonyms: meticulous, scrupulous.

en: Calm and unemotional; not easily excited
hook: PHLEGMATIC: slow and calm, like thick PHLEGM.
story: When the plane hit turbulence and passengers screamed, the phlegmatic old man kept reading his newspaper, sipping his tea calmly. Phlegmatic means calm and unexcitable. Ancient doctors thought too much phlegm made people sluggish and calm.

en: Remarkably impressive in size, extent, or degree
hook: PRODIGIOUS: like a PRODIGY, extraordinary.
story: The young girl had a prodigious memory: she could recite five hundred digits of pi and every word from a book after reading it once. Prodigious means enormous or extraordinary. A prodigious appetite eats three plates of biryani.

en: A natural tendency to behave in a particular way
hook: PROPENSITY: a PRONE tendency.
story: Rafi has a propensity for losing things: keys, wallets, phones, umbrellas. His mother now attaches everything to his bag. Propensity means a natural tendency. Synonyms: proclivity, predilection, inclination.

en: A feeling of doubt or unease, especially about one's conduct
hook: QUALM: a small QUALITY check of your conscience.
story: Mitu had no qualms about telling her boss the truth, even though it was uncomfortable. Her colleague, however, had qualms about lying for him. A qualm is an uneasy feeling of doubt, often moral. Having no qualms means feeling no guilt.

en: To go back on a promise or agreement
hook: RENEGE: RE-NEG(ATE) your promise.
story: The company promised all employees a bonus at Eid, then reneged at the last minute, blaming 'market conditions.' To renege is to break a promise. Synonyms: default, back out. A person who reneges loses trust.

en: Ungenerous; restricting in amount
hook: STINTING: giving only a tiny STINT.
story: The stinting landlord gave the tenants water only two hours a day and switched off the generator at ten. Stinting means ungenerous or restricting. The more common form is unstinting, meaning generous: unstinting praise, unstinting support.

en: To moderate or soften the intensity of something
hook: GRE trick: to TEMPER is to TONE DOWN, like tempering spicy food with yogurt.
story: The teacher tempered her criticism with kindness: 'Your essay has problems, but your ideas are brilliant.' Mitu tempered the spicy curry with yogurt. On the GRE, to temper means to moderate or soften. Tempered steel is hardened, but tempered words are softened.

en: Not certain or fixed; hesitant
hook: TENTATIVE: like a TENT, temporary, not permanent.
story: The wedding date is tentative, maybe December, maybe January, depending on the venue. The baby took a few tentative steps before falling into his mother's arms. Tentative means not definite, or hesitant.

en: Never done or known before
hook: UN-PRECEDENT-ED: no PRECEDENT, never happened before.
story: The 2020 pandemic brought unprecedented changes: whole countries locked down, schools moved online, and streets emptied for months. Nothing like it had happened in living memory. Unprecedented means never seen before.

en: Lively and full of energy, especially in personality
hook: VIVACIOUS: full of VIVA (life).
story: Sara's vivacious grandmother danced at every wedding, told jokes to strangers, and outlasted the young people at every party. Vivacious means attractively lively and animated. Synonyms: effervescent, ebullient, spirited.
